slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: A direct proof starts from what is given and moves one step at a time to the conclusion. Each step needs a reason: a given, a definition, a property, or something already proved.

geo.title: The big idea
geo.body: A direct proof starts from what is given and moves one step at a time to the conclusion. Each step needs a reason: a given, a definition, a property, or something already proved.

slides.title: Words to know
slides.html:
• given A fact we are told to accept at the start of a proof.
  • prove The statement the proof must reach.
  • definition An exact meaning we can use as a reason in a proof.
  • property A rule that numbers or shapes always follow, used as a reason.
  • integers add to integers Adding two integers (positive, negative or zero) always gives another integer.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Prove: if m and n are multiples of 2, then m + n is a multiple of 2.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
m = 2r and n = 2s, for some integers r and s.Definition of a multiple of 2.
m + n = 2r + 2s.Substitution.
2r + 2s = 2(r + s).Distributive property.
r + s is an integer.Adding two integers gives an integer.
So m + n is a multiple of 2.Definition of a multiple of 2.
Second check: m - n = 2(r - s). Since r and s are integers, r - s is an integer by closure under subtraction. Thus m - n is a multiple of 2.A parallel result about the difference, not a second proof of the sum. Subtraction needs its own closure reason.

steps.step: So m + n is a multiple of 2.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Prove: if u and v are odd, then u + v is even.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
u = 2a + 1 and v = 2b + 1, for some integers a and b.Definition of odd.
u + v = 2a + 2b + 2.Add and combine.
u + v = 2(a + b + 1).Distributive property.
a + b + 1 is an integer.Adding integers gives an integer.
So u + v is even.Definition of even.
Second check: an odd number leaves remainder 1 when divided by 2, and 1 + 1 leaves remainder 0.A second way to see it.

slides.title: Try it
slides.html: Proof shuffle: drag scrambled proof lines into order. A line locks in only when every reason it needs is above it.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Kim writes true facts in a random order: 'm + n = 2(r + s). m = 2r. So m + n is even. n = 2s.'

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

A proof is a chain. Each line must follow from lines above it. Put the definitions first, then the algebra, then the conclusion.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
Prove: if m and n are multiples of 4, then m + n is a multiple of 4.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

m = 4r and n = 4s for integers r and s (definition of a multiple). m + n = 4r + 4s = 4(r + s) (substitution, distributive property). r + s is an integer, so m + n is a multiple of 4.

Reveal second check

m - n = 4(r - s). Since r and s are integers, r - s is an integer by closure under subtraction. Thus m - n is a multiple of 4. We used only definitions and properties, not sample numbers.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Find the mistake: from x² = y², Zoe 'cancels the squares' and says x = y for all real numbers x and y.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

She forgot the negative case. x = 2 and y = -2 give x² = y² = 4, but x is not equal to y. The correct conclusion: x = y or x = -y.

Reveal second check

x² - y² = (x - y)(x + y) = 0, so one of the factors is 0. That gives the two cases.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
A proof ends with the right equation, but its first line assumes the thing it is trying to prove. Is it a valid proof? What has to change?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. A conclusion cannot be its own unproved premise. Start from the givens and justify each step. Alternatively, prove that the desired conclusion is equivalent to a statement already known to be true under the givens, with every reverse step justified. Reversibility alone, without a known-true endpoint, is not a proof. (In plain words: steps that run backward can link two false statements, so the chain must end at something you already know is true.)

Reveal second check

If the conclusion were false, this 'assume it first' method would still start the same way. So it can't tell true from false.
